content:
Trump’s agriculture secretary has a habit of sending agency employees explicitly Christian messages. Now a federal judge is telling her to knock it off.

In a preliminary injunction issued Thursday, U.S. District Judge Trina L. Thompson ordered USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins to stop proselytizing through email. Rollins, Thompson wrote, “must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages.”

Up until now, that hasn’t been the case.

Last December, Rollins sent all USDA employees a Christmas note that could have come from a pastor: “The spirit of generosity flows from the very first Christmas when God gave us the greatest gift possible, the gift of his Son and our Savior Jesus Christ, who came to free us from our sins and open the door to eternal life.”

In April, she sent an Easter note addressed to “Team USDA” that began “He is risen indeed!” Rollins went on to celebrate “the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind,” and compared her underlings to “the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord . . . almost two thousand years ago.”

A group of USDA workers and their union, the National Federation of Federal Employees, sued the agency earlier this year arguing that Rollins’ religious missives violated the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause, which bars the government from establishing an official religion. They said Rollins’ emails amounted to indoctrination and coercion.

“The denominational favoritism conveyed in Secretary Rollins’s communications indoctrinates USDA employees and has caused them to feel coerced, unwelcome, excluded, and like outsiders to the agency,” the employees argued in their complaint.

Thompson wrote in her order that she was not trying to “regulate the religiosity of the Secretary,” but instead to get Rollins to “observe her own directives.” Rollins had issued a memo outlining USDA employees’ rights to religious expression at work — rights that Rollins herself was violating by pressuring employees with her own Christian beliefs.

“This Court’s judgment says nothing about the value of prayer or those who believe in its power,” Thompson wrote. “Precisely because the tradition of worship and prayer is so personal and so cherished, protecting private devotion and spiritual reflection from government influence comes to the fore.”

A USDA spokesperson called the order “a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary.”

“[T]he Department is evaluating all options including a prompt appeal,” the spokesperson said in an email.

The workers in the lawsuit are represented by the group Americans United for Separation of Church and State and the legal nonprofit Democracy Forward, which has filed a slew of lawsuits against the Trump administration.

Ashley Miller, a USDA employee who’s among the plaintiffs, said in a statement that they were “heartened and relieved” to see the injunction.

“It was quite scary to come forward,” Miller said, “but I am proud that we did so, knowing this will help everyone across USDA.”

This story has been updated with a response from USDA.
